memory_candidates.content: When a shell-test-suite timing assertion measures wall-clock elapsed time (e.g. 'parallel run finishes under N ms'), an ABSOLUTE millisecond threshold is not robust on a shared development machine: unrelated concurrent processes (other agent sessions, builds, pytest runs) can inflate wall-clock measurements by 2-3x transiently, causing a correct implementation to flake. The fix is a RELATIVE ratio: measure the two conditions being compared (e.g. parallel vs. forced-sequential) back-to-back in the same test run, and assert a ratio between them (e.g. parallel_ms <= 75% of sequential_ms) rather than either an absolute ceiling or floor. This is more robust than an absolute threshold but is NOT unconditionally load-proof: under sufficiently extreme, sustained ambient contention (e.g. 5+ concurrent agent sessions on one machine), even the relative ratio can fail to show a speedup, because the host has no genuinely free cores to parallelize onto. When that happens, the correct response is to report the gate result honestly (the parallelism feature stays opt-in, not default) rather than loosening the test further to force a pass on one specific overloaded host.

When adding an opt-in gate-selection or scope-reduction flag to a verifier/battery script (e.g. --only-gate N to skip N-1 of N checks), do a full cross-check-variable dependency audit BEFORE wiring the guard -- read every check block and confirm no later check reads a variable an earlier, now-skippable check assigns. If the audit finds zero cross-dependencies (common when each check is written as a self-contained block with uniquely-named local variables), the guard can be added mechanically (wrap each block in 'if selected(N); then ... fi' without reindenting the body) with high confidence and a small, reviewable diff. Verify empirically too: run every individual selection standalone and confirm none crashes with an unbound-variable or unset-path error -- this is the regression net for the audit's own correctness.

A cheap, rigorous coverage-equality proof for 'did this change reduce test coverage' does not require re-running an entire pre-change test suite: git diff --stat against the commit immediately before the change set shows exactly which suite files were touched. Every untouched file is coverage-unchanged BY CONSTRUCTION (its behavior cannot have changed since its bytes did not change), which only needs stating, not re-executing. For the small set of actually-modified files, diff pass/fail assertion call-site counts (e.g. grep -c 'pass "' / 'fail "') before (git show <old-commit>:<path>) vs. after (current file) to prove zero assertions were silently dropped. New files are purely additive coverage by definition. This is both cheaper and more rigorous than re-running the full old suite for comparison, since it proves invariance structurally rather than relying on two potentially-flaky executions to agree.
